title: Read a reference script on nine points before outlining
when: Before writing an original script in a format learned from a reference video's title and transcript.
summary: Analyse the reference first and outline second. The analysis names why the format works so the new script can borrow the reasons, never the words. The outline only starts after a new topic is chosen.
steps: Script type: list, story, how-to, commentary, explainer or another form.
Audience: who the topic and delivery serve, and what they want from it.
Storytelling devices: suspense, open loops, personal experience, case examples.
Tone, structure and format: pace, emotional register, section order.
Hook: what happens in the first 5-10 seconds and whether it earns the next minute.
Direct address: how the script talks to the viewer and builds closeness.
Retention: what keeps people watching through the middle.
Psychological triggers: curiosity, authority, trust, mystery, contrast.
Spread potential: which elements make the video likely to be shared, and why.
do: Record the reference word count so the new outline can size itself against it.
Ask for the new topic only after the analysis is accepted.
avoid: Starting without both the title and the full transcript.
Reusing any sentence, signature phrase or named example from the reference.
checks: All nine points cite evidence from the transcript, not impressions.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 1-9 (owner course material, restated in our words)

title: Expand an outline one section at a time, to its allocation
when: When an approved outline is turned into narration section by section.
summary: Long scripts stay on target when each outline section is expanded on its own, to its allocated length, continuing the tone of the section before. Narration carries no headings, scene notes or voice cues, and the next section waits for a go-ahead.

inputs.summary: What the section covers and the feeling it should leave

steps: Restate the section's purpose and intended viewer feeling in one line before writing.
Write only this section: open with a hook, end on a line that leads into the next section.
Count the words and adjust until the section sits on its allocation.
Stop and wait for the next section; never write ahead.
do: Keep tone and pacing continuous with the previous section.
Use the contrast the outline assigns to this section.
avoid: Subheadings, scene ideas, visual cues or voice-over directions inside narration.
Filler or repetition used to reach the count.
Writing several sections in one pass.
checks: Section length is within 3 percent of its allocation. The course asks for exact counts; the program accepts 3 percent and flags more.
The section ends on a forward link, not full closure.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 2-3, 18-22, 36-38, 426-428 (owner course material, restated)

title: Chapter and section word allocation that adds up exactly
when: When outlining a script longer than about 3,000 words, especially multi-hour sleep and documentary formats.
summary: Size the script from runtime, split it into chapters and sections, and make every number add up: sections to their chapter, chapters to the target. Each section carries a name, its allocation, a summary and the feeling it should leave.
steps: Convert runtime to words at 150-170 words a minute (rule wordsForMinutes, default 155).
Pick a chapter count that suits the story, for example 10 chapters of 3,000 words for 30,000.
Split each chapter into sections and give each an exact allocation.
Write each section summary: what happens, why it is there, and the viewer state it should leave (curiosity, dread, calm, empathy).
Run the allocation check and fix any chapter or total that does not add up before writing begins.
do: Give long-form section summaries real substance so expansion does not drift.
Plan a contrast and a transition at every section boundary.
avoid: Rounded or approximate totals.
Equal-length sections by default when the story needs a longer climax.
checks: wordAllocationIssues finds no mismatch in the outline.
Every section names a purpose and an intended viewer feeling.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 16-18, 137-141, 167-436 (owner course material, restated)

title: Contrast framing: alternate registers so the listener feels movement
when: Whenever an outline or a section is written, in any niche.
summary: Engagement comes from alternation. Pair opposites across and inside sections, such as emotional against analytical, before against after, evidence against speculation, calm against disturbing, so the listener feels movement without being jolted.
steps: Name the contrast pair the niche runs on before outlining.
Give each section a side of the pair, or a turn between them.
Inside a section, follow an emotional or high-energy beat with a short analytical one.
do: In sleep formats, keep the contrast in ideas, never in volume or sudden shocks.
avoid: One register for a whole section.
Contrast that bends facts to create drama.
checks: Each section boundary shows a named contrast or turn.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 18-22, 47-55, 424 and the niche packs (owner course material, restated)

title: Invisible hooks: small open questions on a steady rhythm
when: When placing retention hooks through a long script.
summary: Hooks work best when the viewer does not notice them as hooks. End sections on a small unanswered question, open a new curiosity loop at a steady interval, and never close a scene completely before the next one begins.
steps: Close each section on a mini cliffhanger or an unanswered hint.
In mystery formats, open a new loop every 300-400 words.
In calm sleep formats, place a gentle transitional hook about every 700 words, roughly every ten minutes.
Track every open loop and pay it off later.
avoid: Loud teasers or shock lines in sleep content.
Loops that are never paid off.
Fake suspense about facts that are already settled.
checks: Every opened loop is paid off before the end.
No section except the last ends in full closure.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 35-36, 122-126, 136, 395 (owner course material, restated)

title: Capture the owner's own view before the script is written
when: Before a researched or documentary script is drafted, so it carries a human point of view and not only compiled facts.
summary: Original value is the best defence against reused or low-effort content. Ask the owner a short set of sharp questions about framing, responsibility, impact and the lesson, and write the script around those answers. The answers are the author's view; the research is the foundation.
steps: Draft up to ten questions covering framing, responsibility, emotional impact, damage to identity or reputation, long-term consequences, the lesson to imply, and the ending tone.
Wait for the owner's answers; do not proceed on guesses.
Use the answers to choose the angle, the order of revelations and the closing note.
Keep fact, interpretation and the owner's opinion visibly separate in the script.
do: Quote the owner's framing in the outline so reviewers can see where the angle came from.
avoid: Inventing the owner's opinions.
Presenting the owner's interpretation as established fact.
checks: The outline names which owner answer drives the angle and the ending.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 sessions, pp. 448-451 (owner course material, restated)

title: Build the audience and script report before a family's first scripts
when: When a family starts in a niche, before its first outline prompt is settled.
summary: Scripts land when they are written for a known audience. Read two transcripts from two different competitors and the top comments under their most-watched videos, write a report on who watches and why, and only then build the outline and expansion prompts on that report.
steps: Collect two transcripts from two different competitors and the strongest comments under each one's most-watched video.
From comments: age, situation, desires, pains and the words viewers use about themselves.
From transcripts: tone, structure, format, type and style, each in one line.
Write the report, then the outline prompt (target length, sections with allocations, contrast, transitions), then the expansion prompt.
Test both prompts on one title and one section before using them for a series.
avoid: Treating one competitor as the whole audience.
Copying commenters' words into scripts or titles.
checks: The report names the audience's pains and desires in plain words, with comment evidence.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 46-50, 66-69 (owner course material, restated)

title: Dark philosophy documentary arc
when: For a family making 20-30 minute philosophy and psychology documentaries in a thriller-like register.
summary: The video should feel like a psychological thriller, not a lecture. Open on tension, move through a historical reference to the psychology behind it, connect it to a modern problem, and end on a message the viewer keeps.
steps: Hook: a tense question or scene that challenges how the viewer sees something ordinary.
History: a real, sourced historical reference that shows the pattern at work.
Psychology: explain the mechanism behind the pattern in plain words.
Today: connect it to a problem the viewer lives with now.
Close: one clear message, stated calmly.
do: Write conversationally but with depth.
Give each outline section a 200-300 word summary so expansion stays on course.
avoid: Presenting conspiracy or speculation as fact.
Generalisations that demean a group of people.
checks: Every historical claim has a named source.
The arc reaches a modern application before the close.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 23-25 (owner course material, restated)

title: Immersive bedtime history in the second person
when: For a family making calm history storytelling meant to help listeners relax or sleep.
summary: Put the listener inside ordinary life in another era, as 'you', with sensory detail and honest history. The voice is a knowledgeable, gentle historian talking to a curious friend; calm comes from steady pacing, not from vagueness.
steps: Open with an emotional scene that places the listener in the era.
Move through daily life: work, food, danger, belief, family, told through the senses.
Place a soft transitional hook about every 700 words.
Add a gentle invitation to comment or share a thought about every ten minutes.
End quietly, with reflection rather than a twist.
do: Use moderate sentence length and occasional rhetorical questions or pauses.
Blend fact with empathy, and keep the facts checkable.
avoid: Jargon, shock, sudden energy changes.
Banned filler such as 'stay tuned' in the invitations.
checks: Point of view stays in the second person throughout.
No section contains a jarring image or loud claim.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 35-38 (owner course material, restated)

title: Sleep documentary segment: measured, chronological, calm
when: For a family making multi-hour documentaries designed to inform and help viewers fall asleep.
summary: Each segment is a calm, third-person, chronological unit that fits a 2-4 hour whole. Authority comes from precise dates, names and places; calm comes from measured pacing and the absence of intensifiers.
steps: Context: place the event in its wider history.
Background: causes and the events that led to it.
Main narrative: the events in strict order.
Analysis: key decisions and the different readings historians give.
Consequences: the immediate results.
Transition: a gentle bridge to the next segment.
do: Write sentences that are clear when heard.
Use natural pauses in sentence structure rather than dramatic words.
avoid: Sensational language, sudden revelations, harsh imagery.
Opinion presented as historical consensus.
checks: Events are in chronological order.
Every date, name and place can be traced to a source.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 113-115, 121-127 (owner course material, restated)

title: 1,000-word problem-to-solution explainer
when: For a family making short self-improvement explainers that end in one action the viewer can take today.
summary: Six sections move the viewer from feeling understood to acting. The allocation below adds up to 1,000; the course example adds up to 1,050, which is exactly the kind of drift the allocation check exists to catch.
steps: Hook and topic: name the pain and promise what the viewer will be able to do.
Problem: describe the struggle with one relatable example.
Solution introduced: the idea that changes it, without giving every step away.
Steps: two or three concrete, achievable techniques.
Act now: one small challenge for today.
Close: a short summary and an encouraging last line.
do: Use before-and-after contrast.
Keep each step something a viewer could do in five minutes.
avoid: Fake urgency piled on every section.
Banned filler such as 'stay tuned'.
Health or money promises the evidence does not support.
checks: Allocation adds up to 1,000.
The viewer leaves with one specific action.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 51-57 (owner course material, restated and corrected)

title: Named-step short with one tip per step
when: For a family making fast, high-energy short explainers built from a handful of named techniques.
summary: A bold opening claim, four to six steps each with a memorable name, a short real-world example, an actionable tip and a micro-tip, then a light close. Specific numbers and sensory cues make it stick; authority must be real.
steps: Hook in the first 15 seconds: a bold, true claim about the result.
For each of 4-6 steps: a catchy name, a short sourced example, the tip, a micro-tip, one sensory cue.
Close with a clear ask and a light, human line.
do: Speak to 'you' in the active voice with direct instructions.
Use specific numbers only when a source supports them.
avoid: Invented authority such as claims that a spy agency or famous lab used the method.
Words like secret, leaked or banned when nothing is secret or banned.
Technical jargon.
checks: Every authority claim names a real, checkable source or is removed.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, p. 32 (owner course material, restated with the fabricated-authority device removed)

title: True crime written in parts that each end unresolved
when: For a family making documentary scripts about real, closed criminal cases.
summary: Write the case in parts of a few hundred words, each opening on a hook and ending on a question, so the viewer keeps going. Everything factual comes from court records and established news coverage, and the people involved are treated with respect.
steps: Cold open: a chilling but true sentence that signals something is wrong.
Introduce the people and situation.
Add investigative depth: police work, evidence, trial, money, betrayal, each from a cited source.
End the part on an unanswered question that leads into the next.
do: Name the source behind each fact (judgment, prosecution service, national news).
Use plain, powerful English.
avoid: Framing a case around the ethnicity, nationality or immigration status of the people involved.
Speculating about guilt beyond the verdict, or naming people not charged.
Graphic detail that adds shock but no understanding.
checks: Every name, date and sum is traceable to a cited source.
Each part except the last ends on an open question.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 132-136 (owner course material, restated; ethnicity framing excluded)

title: Self-improvement explainer: eight internal beats, no guru tone
when: For a family making calm, serious explainers about discipline, focus, confidence and direction.
summary: The viewer should feel understood, challenged and clearer. Follow eight beats internally, in flowing paragraphs with no headings, and let every paragraph move the idea forward.
steps: Open with a sharp truth or a misunderstood reality.
Make the viewer feel personally seen.
Explain the hidden reason behind the problem.
Break down the behaviour or mindset in simple language.
Show how it quietly damages life.
Contrast weak patterns with stronger ones.
Offer a deeper shift in perspective.
End on one clean, memorable truth.
do: Use everyday examples.
Keep one dominant idea per video.
avoid: Headings, bullet points, visual or voice directions in the narration.
Guru tone, fake motivation, spiritual filler, repeated points.
checks: No paragraph repeats an earlier point.
The ending states the idea in one sentence.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 session, pp. 459-461 (owner course material, restated)

title: Investigative business documentary: fact, interpretation, perception
when: For a family making neutral 12-15 minute documentaries about a company's decisions and their consequences.
summary: Authority comes from restraint. Research from primary business sources, separate what is proven from what is debated, add the owner's framing, and tell the story in a fixed shape that ends cold and analytical.
steps: Open on a symbolic turning point.
Rewind to the period of dominance.
Introduce the structural pressures.
Explain why the decision made sense at the time.
Show where it failed, citing evidence.
Close with a restrained business insight.
do: Label every claim as fact, interpretation or public perception.
Say plainly when cause and effect is not proven.
avoid: Ideology, exaggeration and a call to action at the end.
Visual or voice directions inside the script.
checks: No causal claim appears without evidence.
The research brief lists its sources.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 session, pp. 448-451 (owner course material, restated)

title: Plain-language explainer outline in the second person
when: For a family making informative explainers that must be easy for a wide audience to follow.
summary: Ask for the topic, the unique angle and any must-include points; then outline a hook, three to five main points each opened by a curiosity loop and explained in short complete thoughts, and a payoff that says how to apply it.
steps: Collect the topic, the unique angle and the owner's own points.
Hook: a short attention-grabbing opening.
Body: 3-5 points, each with an open loop and 4-6 short bullets of complete thoughts.
Payoff: what the viewer learned and how to use it.
Review against the angle and the owner's points.
do: Write at about an eighth-grade reading level: simple words, short sentences.
Speak to 'you' and use examples for hard ideas.
avoid: Losing the unique angle in a generic overview.
checks: The unique angle is visible in the hook and the payoff.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 notes, pp. 441-443 (owner course material, restated)

title: Cross a current trend with the family's niche
when: When a family needs timely ideas without leaving its niche.
summary: Pick one trend that is genuinely current, explain in a line how it connects to the niche, then generate ideas that serve the niche's audience through that trend, each with an opening hook and the editing idea that would carry it.
steps: Confirm the trend is current from the research brief, not from memory.
Write the connection: why this audience cares about this trend.
Generate a batch of ideas that merge the two.
For the strongest ideas, add an opening hook and the editing approach that supports it.
avoid: Exploiting a tragedy or a live conflict for clicks.
Trends whose link to the niche needs a stretch to explain.
checks: The trend is cited with a date.
Each idea is useful to the niche audience even after the trend fades.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, p. 10 (owner course material, restated)

title: Drill a niche into subcategories before writing titles
when: When a family needs a deep, varied list of topics inside one niche.
summary: Generic titles come from generic categories. Break the niche into subcategories and those into narrower ones, choose a specific genre for the channel, then write topics per subcategory, each aimed at one specific pain or question.
steps: Study competitor titles to describe the niche, its audience and its subcategories.
Split each subcategory again until each branch names a specific audience problem.
Pick the channel's own genre inside the tree.
Write topics per branch, then titles per topic.
avoid: Titles that could belong to any channel in the niche.
checks: Each title names a specific problem, situation or audience.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 58-60, 66-67 (owner course material, restated)

title: Every title proposal carries its reason
when: Whenever titles are proposed for review.
summary: A reviewer can only judge a title when it says why it should work. Each proposal carries a one-line reason grounded in audience psychology or click behaviour, and borrows patterns from competitors, never their phrases.
do: Give each title one reason: the curiosity gap, the emotion, the audience problem it names.
Mix structures across the list.
avoid: Copying a competitor's title or signature phrase.
Words that need to be avoided for advertiser safety.
checks: Every title has a reason.
titleVariationIssues finds no repeated opening pattern.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, niche packs pp. 167-436 (owner course material, restated)

title: Core ideas to topics to titles, with variation rules
when: When generating a batch of titles for a channel that publishes often in one niche.
summary: Titles stay original when they come down a ladder: a few core ideas, each with a different emotional or conceptual angle; several specific topics under each; one hand-written-feeling title per topic. Variation rules stop the batch looking templated.
steps: Write 6-8 core ideas, each on a different angle (atmosphere, experience, emotion, format).
Under each, write 4-6 specific topics that differ in scene, mood, time or perspective.
Write one title per topic, matching the niche's length and rhythm.
Rotate phrasing between point-of-view, descriptive, invitational and observational.
Run the variation check; rewrite anything generic or repetitive.
avoid: The same opening more than twice in a row.
Keyword stuffing.
One structure across a whole channel.
checks: titleVariationIssues returns no issues.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 session, pp. 445-446 (owner course material, restated)

title: Small-channel outlier signals for a niche worth entering
when: When the Niche Factory screens candidate niches from NexLev or the owner's ideas.
summary: A niche is promising when young, small channels already get steady views in a format we can produce. These thresholds come from the course and are starting points, not proven rules; the Niche Factory records the evidence behind each.
steps: Find channels that are young and small but average healthy views.
Check that the format and video length are ones we can produce.
Collect about 15 channels with a similar format across the main niche and its sub-niches, then shortlist 5.
On a shortlisted channel, study the editing format on its oldest videos, then the most popular, then the newest.
do: Record each threshold as a course heuristic in the evaluation, with the measured value beside it.
avoid: Treating a single viral video as a niche.

numbers.competitor_age: about 3-6 months for fresh niches; at least 6 months for proven ones
numbers.video_length_minutes: 40-240 for long-form sleep and documentary formats
numbers.label: course heuristic, unverified

checks: The evaluation states the measured values, not only pass or fail.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 149, 435, 439 (owner course material, restated)

title: Choose a niche by format, subcategory and audience
when: When a niche idea is too broad to brief a channel.
summary: A niche is a category, and categories are too wide to win. Fix three things: the format (how the videos are made), the subcategory (narrowed until it names one audience), and the audience itself.
steps: Name the format.
Narrow the subject step by step, the way 'teacher' narrows to 'maths teacher' and then to 'maths for one school year'.
Describe the audience the narrowest subcategory serves.
checks: The niche statement names a format, a narrow subcategory and an audience.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 'Niches in a Nutshell', p. 435 (owner course material, restated)

title: Concepts that could not be shown before AI
when: When the Niche Factory looks for original channel concepts the stock-plus-AI pipeline can produce.
summary: Much of history, nature and human life exists only in text and was never filmed or painted. Concepts that make such material visible, or place a familiar figure in an unfamiliar time, can be produced entirely from stock and AI images.
steps: List subjects documented in writing but rarely visualised.
Generate many concepts, then keep about 50 with sample titles.
Branch into specific animals, places, trades and daily routines for depth.
Check each concept can be produced with our stock and AI image providers before it goes to review.
avoid: Concepts that need real footage of real people.
Concepts whose appeal is a celebrity likeness.
checks: Each kept concept names how its visuals would be produced.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 131-132 (owner course material, restated)

title: Keep the format, change the market
when: When a proven format is found and the family wants a fresh market for it.
summary: Replicate the container, never the content. Take a format that works, explain why it works, and carry it into new markets where the same psychological pull exists, building a fresh angle for each. This extends niche.niche-bending with a market list.
steps: Describe the format: length, structure, visual style, voice, pacing.
State why it works for its audience.
List about ten markets with the same underlying pull.
For the best, write a unique angle and ten first video ideas.
avoid: Moving the competitor's topics, wording or identity into the new market.
checks: Each new market states its own audience and angle.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, Content DNA Engine, pp. 456-457, 465-472 (owner course material, restated)

title: Forensic read of why a channel is growing
when: When a competitor grows fast with few uploads and the family wants to understand why before learning from it.
summary: Explain why, not only what. Require the inputs first, read the channel through its true niche, emotional promise, audience psychology, hooks, thumbnails, structure, script, visuals and business model, then explain why viewers click, stay and binge, and split what to learn from what to avoid.
steps: Stop until the inputs exist: channel, goal of the analysis, most-watched video, two or three transcripts, and the about text.
Name the true niche beyond its label and the emotional promise to the viewer.
Read hooks and titles, thumbnails, structure, script framework, visuals and editing pace, and how it earns.
Explain why it grows: click-through, retention and what makes viewers binge.
List what to learn (systems) and what to avoid (identity, wording, signature look).
avoid: Surface observations without a reason.
Over-focus on tools.
checks: Every conclusion carries its reasoning.
The learn list contains no competitor wording or signature.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 sessions, pp. 448-449, 465-472 (owner course material, restated)

title: Extract the core ideas behind a competitor's topics
when: When a competitor's viral topics should inform the family's idea buckets without copying them.
summary: Under every viral topic is an abstract idea that could serve other subjects. Extract it, explain why it resonates, and turn it into a repeatable theme bucket for the family. No titles at this stage.
steps: For each topic, state the abstract core idea.
Explain why it resonates psychologically.
Say which other subjects or markets it fits.
Turn it into a named theme bucket.
avoid: Generating titles in this step.
Buckets that are just the competitor's topics renamed.
checks: Each bucket can produce topics outside the competitor's subject.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 sessions, pp. 449, 456 (owner course material, restated)

title: Decode a competitor's editing pattern and its alternatives
when: When a reference channel's editing should inform a family's style.
summary: Read the editing as a system: what kinds of visuals, how often the picture changes, the music, the captions, the visual hooks, the template and the search terms that would find similar material. Then ask which other formats could tell the same topics, because format is where saturation happens.
steps: Classify visuals: stock, AI images, animation, typography, archival.
Measure how many seconds each visual holds, at the start and in the middle.
Note music style and how it follows the narration.
Note captions, text overlays and fonts.
Describe visual hooks in the first 30 seconds.
Write the editing template as a short recipe.
List other formats that could carry the same topics, such as stick figure, whiteboard, map-led or typography.
avoid: Copying a signature look; learn the technique, not the identity.
checks: The template states the change cadence in seconds.
At least two alternative formats are named.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 43-45, 69 (owner course material, restated)

title: Build a channel's five-step prompt set from analysis
when: When a family needs its own prompt set after a niche and its references are analysed.
summary: A family's production runs on five prompts: titles, script (outline then expansion), images, thumbnail and SEO. Each is built from analysis of 10-15 recent videos and follows a fixed internal structure so it can be tested and revised.
steps: Title prompt: instruction, niche criteria, audience, tone, hook words, pattern examples, generation variable.
Script prompt: writer role, content type, quality rules, structure with word counts, phased go-ahead, engagement devices, restrictions.
Image prompt: visual style, colour and light, mood, subject elements, technical spec, output format.
Thumbnail prompt: style, composition, colour and contrast, brand consistency, subject, final spec.
SEO prompt: tags, description, alternative titles, keyword strategy.
Test each prompt on one example before it is used for a series.
avoid: Generic prompts that would fit any channel.
Examples copied from the analysed channel into the prompt.
checks: Every variable in each prompt is marked and listed.
Each prompt passed one test run.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 66-70, 431-434 (owner course material, restated)

title: Sweep public discussion for sentiment and counterpoints
when: When a topic is current and the brief needs to know how people are discussing it.
summary: Read how a topic is discussed across news, verified voices and social platforms: the main conversations, sentiment, influential reactions, hashtags, counterpoints and how regions differ. Everything gathered is opinion unless it is a reported fact with a source.
steps: Summarise the main discussions and where they happen.
Record overall sentiment and the reasons behind it.
Capture reactions from verified experts and officials, with links.
List counterpoints and debates.
Compare how different regions or camps frame it.
avoid: Treating viral posts as facts.
Quoting private individuals.
checks: Each reaction or figure carries a source link and date.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 13-15 (owner course material, restated)

title: Separate proven, debated and inconclusive in every brief
when: Whenever a research brief feeds a documentary, case or business script.
summary: A brief earns trust when it shows what kind of claim each line is. Prefer primary sources, mark each point as proven, debated or inconclusive, and say so plainly when causation is not established.
do: Prefer primary sources: filings, court records, official reports, recorded statements.
Use established news outlets for context and dates.
Mark each claim proven, debated or inconclusive.
avoid: Turning correlation into cause.
Presenting an analyst's opinion as a finding.
checks: Every claim in the brief carries its status and a source.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 session, p. 449; UK case sourcing pp. 132-134 (owner course material, restated)

title: Every image prompt names the script line it illustrates
when: Whenever image prompts are generated from narration.
summary: An image is only useful if the edit knows where it goes. Each prompt carries the exact script words it belongs to, so the scene plan and the Editing Room can place it on the right moment of the voice-over.
do: Quote the exact narration words after each prompt.
Number prompts in script order.
avoid: Prompts grouped by mood with no anchor in the script.
checks: Every prompt has a script anchor that exists verbatim in the narration.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 27, 39-40 (owner course material, restated)

title: Extract non-generic keywords in six groups
when: When a paragraph of narration needs stock searches or image prompts.
summary: Stock searches fail on generic words. Pull specific keywords from the paragraph and group them as people, places, events, objects, emotions and concepts, dropping duplicates and anything too generic to find a distinctive result.
steps: Read the paragraph for its story, not only its nouns.
Group keywords: people, places, events, objects, emotions, concepts.
Drop generic words unless the context makes them specific, and remove duplicates.
Turn the strongest into short stock queries and prompt subjects.
avoid: One-word queries like 'man' or 'city'.
The same keyword across consecutive paragraphs.
checks: No keyword repeats within the paragraph's list.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 43, 63-65 (owner course material, restated)

title: Structured image prompts that follow the script's flow
when: When writing AI image prompts for a narrated video.
summary: Prompts stay consistent when they share fields: scene, main element, secondary element, background, style, tone, lighting, camera and atmosphere. Generate them as one continuous sequence that follows the narration, not grouped by hook or climax.
steps: Fix the style, palette, lighting family and period once for the whole video.
For each moment: scene, main element, secondary element, background, camera framing, atmosphere.
Keep each prompt vivid but compact.
Check consecutive prompts look like the same film.
avoid: Labelling prompts by script section instead of following the narrative rhythm.
Text inside images.
checks: All prompts share the locked style fields.
Framing varies across neighbours.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 380, 391, 401-402, 421 (owner course material, restated)

title: Paragraph tiers decide how many images a paragraph gets
when: For a family whose style counts images per paragraph instead of per fixed word interval.
summary: Some styles size images by paragraph length using a tier table. The family's style names which table it uses; the count is computed in code with paragraphImageCount, and a tier marked 'ask' needs owner confirmation first.
steps: Count the paragraph's words.
Look up the family's tier table.
If the tier says ask, confirm the count with the owner before generating.
Generate exactly that many prompts, each anchored to a script line.
checks: The prompt count equals paragraphImageCount for the family's table.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 26-28, 40, 70, 172, 205, 366 (owner course material, restated)

title: Lock a period look and keep every frame inside it
when: For a family whose visual identity is a historical photographic or painted look.
summary: A period look only convinces if nothing breaks it. Fix the era, the medium and its imperfections, and check every prompt for modern objects, colour where there should be none, and lighting the period could not produce.
steps: Choose the look and write it as the family's locked style line.
List what the medium includes (grain, dust, vignetting, brushwork) and what it forbids.
Check each prompt against the forbidden list before generation.

looks.wet_plate_1900_1930: black and white only, low-key light, grain, dust and scratches, vignette, period clothing
looks.archival_1940s: true black and white 35mm, overcast or tungsten light, smoke and fog, humane and sombre, never heroic
looks.victorian_edwardian_1880_1915: black and white studio portrait feel, ornate interiors, minimal grain
looks.hand_painted_vintage: soft brushwork, muted earthy colours, 18th-19th century illustration
looks.classical_oil: renaissance-inspired realism, wide or close-up framing, no text
looks.expressive_oil_sketch: raw visible brushstrokes, emotional tension, unfinished movement

avoid: Modern objects, neon, HDR or colour grading foreign to the era.
Identifiable real people rendered by AI.
checks: No prompt contains an element the locked look forbids.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 26-28, 39-40, 390-392, 410-421, 428-429 (owner course material, restated)

title: Short AI video clips planned as timed beats
when: Only for a family that uses AI video, and only after the AI video adapter is built and tested; until then this stays unused.
summary: An 8-10 second AI clip works when it is one moment with timed beats: hook, context, climax, resolution, each with its camera move, sound and emotion. Image-to-video from an approved still keeps continuity better than text alone.
steps: Generate and approve the base still first.
Plan beats: 0-3 s hook, 3-6 s context, 6-8 s climax, 8-10 s resolution.
For each beat: camera move, subtle realistic motion, sound, emotion.
Keep one moment per clip and one period and style across the series.
avoid: Real people's likeness, including religious figures and celebrities.
Realistic fake security or doorbell footage presented as real.
Undisclosed synthetic media.
checks: The AI video capability is enabled for the family before this is used.
The upload carries the altered or synthetic content disclosure.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 91-98, 156-166 (owner course material, restated; likeness and fake-footage prompts excluded)

title: Every clip comes from stock or approved AI generation
when: Whenever an edit plan names where a visual comes from.
summary: Course prompts often suggest movie scenes, YouTube clips and web images. This program uses only licensed stock libraries and its own AI generation, so the plan maps each of those suggestions to an allowed source or drops it.
do: Map 'movie clip' ideas to stock footage or an AI still with motion.
Record provider, asset ID and licence for each visual.
avoid: Film or TV clips, YouTube or social downloads, and images from general web search.
Assets with watermarks, logos or burned-in captions.
checks: Every visual in the plan has an allowed provider and an asset or generation ID.
source: Owner decision (stock and AI only) applied to CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 61-62, 84-85, 430

title: Screenplay breakdown: one block per scene with everything the edit needs
when: When a documentary script is turned into a production plan.
summary: Each scene becomes one block: a header with number, title, duration, narration word count and visual style; the narration; the visual breakdown; the audio; and the transition. The editor should never need to reread the script.
steps: Header: scene number, title, duration, narration words, visual style.
Narration block with emphasis and pause points marked.
Visuals A: stock needs with search terms and clip durations.
Visuals B: 3-5 AI image prompts for the key moments.
Visuals C: graphics and overlays such as place and date stamps, name cards, figures, timelines and maps.
Audio: music style, sound effects, narration pacing and pauses.
Transition: how the scene joins the next, and the retention hook it carries.
checks: Scene durations add up to the narration length.
Every graphic names its data source.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 109-111 (owner course material, restated)

title: Zero-decision assembly package
when: When a still-image documentary is assembled from narration, images and music.
summary: Assembly should need no creative decisions once the plan is approved: numbered images in script order, a computed hold per image, music placed by time range, and a fixed sequence of steps with quality checkpoints.
steps: Confirm title, script, theme, audience, length, image count, style, aspect and mood.
Map the script's emotional beats and transition points.
Compute the hold: narration seconds divided by image count (imageIntervalSeconds), then let the Editing Room lengthen holds on hero beats and shorten them on fast passages.
Number the image prompts 1..N in script order, each anchored to its line.
Pick 3-4 licensed music tracks with start and end times per section.
Write the assembly steps and the QC checkpoints.
avoid: An equal hold for every image across a whole video; vary within the computed average.
checks: Image holds sum to the narration length.
Every music track has a licence record.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 150-155 (owner course material, restated)

title: Fixed-interval clip map for fast-cut styles
when: For a family whose style changes the picture on a fixed short interval.
summary: Fast-cut formats map the script in fixed slots: time, script line, clip type, visual description, editor note with a file name, and search keywords. The map also marks emotional beats, transition points and where a visual metaphor is needed.
steps: Mark narrative flow, emotional beats, climaxes and tone shifts.
Fill one row per slot: time, line, clip type, visual, editor note, keywords.
Name files as scene type plus sequence number.
Add transition, colour, sync point and text overlay notes where they matter.
Propose an alternative sequence for any slow passage.
avoid: Clip types outside the allowed sources (see editing.clip-source-policy).
checks: No slot is empty and no two neighbouring slots use the same asset.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 61-62 (owner course material, restated)

title: Visual pacing for sleep and calm documentaries
when: For a family whose videos are meant to help viewers relax or fall asleep.
summary: Nothing on screen should startle. Use slow cross-dissolves, very slow camera moves on a share of stills, long holds, a dark low-contrast grade, and text only for places, years and ranks.
do: Cross-dissolve between images.
Apply a very slow push or pan to some stills, not all.
Keep text overlays to place names, years and ranks.
avoid: Flash, shake, whip transitions, bright reds or neon.
Sudden loud sound or music changes.

numbers.palette: deep blues and navy, black and white or sepia, low contrast, light vignette

checks: No transition shorter than the dissolve range.
No colour or loudness spike in the review pass.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 115-117, 392 (owner course material, restated)

title: A rotating pool of visuals for multi-hour videos
when: For a family making 2-4 hour calm videos where one visual per sentence would be wasteful.
summary: Long calm videos can rotate a pool of approved images and loopable clips instead of a new visual for every line. The pool still follows the script's chapters and never shows the same asset twice in a row or a single image for the whole video.
steps: Build a pool per chapter from approved stock and AI assets.
Rotate through the pool so no asset appears twice in a row.
Refresh the pool at each chapter so the picture follows the story.
avoid: One image for the whole video.
Reusing the same pool across many videos on a channel.
checks: No two neighbouring placements use the same asset.
Each chapter draws from its own pool.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 131, 441 (owner course material, restated)

title: Rotate editing formats inside a channel
when: When a channel publishes many videos in one style, or when views stall.
summary: Niches rarely saturate; formats do. A channel can publish the same niche and audience in several editing formats, and changing format is one of the three levers when views stall, together with prompts and thumbnails. Rotation also keeps a channel from looking mass-produced.
steps: Keep at least two approved editing styles per family once the first is proven.
Track results per format, not only per video.
When a format tires, change it before changing the niche.
avoid: Dozens of videos in one identical template.
Switching format every video, which prevents learning.
checks: The family's plan names its active formats and when each was last used.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 438, 441, 465, 474 (owner course material, restated)

title: Stick-figure scene breakdown, line by line
when: For a family whose style is simple stick-figure animation.
summary: Every narration line gets a timed scene: the figure's pose and action, minimal props drawn as simple shapes, a simple background, bold hand-drawn text with arrows or symbols, a basic transition and a sound effect. Body language carries emotion; the palette is black, white and one accent.
steps: Give each line a start and end time.
Describe the pose and action in body language, no facial features.
Draw props and backgrounds as basic shapes.
Add bold hand-drawn text with an arrow or symbol where a number or key idea lands.
Choose a simple transition (slide, wipe, small shake on an impact) and one sound effect.
avoid: Detail that slows the read.
More than one accent colour.

numbers.palette: black, white and one accent colour

checks: Every line has a scene and every scene has a time range.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 32-33 (owner course material, restated)

title: Three thumbnail variants that differ on purpose
when: When a thumbnail is designed for review.
summary: Offer three thumbnails that differ in one deliberate dimension each, such as palette, angle or subject, so the review is a real choice. Text is short, readable at phone size, and true to the video.
steps: Variant A, B and C each change one named dimension.
Change exactly one variable per variant (colour, text, expression or composition) and write the hypothesis it tests and the viewers it should win.
Keep text to a few words with high contrast.
Check readability at a phone-sized preview.
avoid: Text claims the video does not support, such as experts being baffled when they are not.
Clutter and more than one focal point.
checks: Every thumbnail claim is supported by the script.
Each variant differs from the primary in one named variable only.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 116-118, 128-130 (owner course material, restated); updated 0.71 from claude-youtube (MIT, 84c3fa6): sub-skills/thumbnail.md

title: Description, tags, alternative titles and chapters in one package
when: When a long-form video's metadata is prepared.
summary: Metadata is one package: a short three-paragraph description, a balanced tag set, a few alternative titles, a keyword list and chronological chapters. Keywords appear naturally, never stuffed.
steps: Paragraph 1: an opening question or statement, the scope, primary keywords in the first two or three sentences.
Paragraph 2: what the viewer will learn, with secondary keywords.
Paragraph 3: the subscription ask, related videos, a few hashtags.
Tags: core channel tags, topic tags with spelling variants, and broader category tags.
Five alternative titles and a keyword list.
Chronological chapter timestamps.
checks: Chapter times match the final render.
No tag is a competitor's channel name.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 118-120 (owner course material, restated)

title: State the channel's own research and AI assistance
when: When a channel description and video descriptions are written.
summary: Say plainly that the ideas and research are the channel's own and that AI tools help with presentation. This supports the authenticity of the work; it never replaces YouTube's altered or synthetic content setting where that applies.
do: Keep a short disclaimer in the channel description.
Use YouTube's synthetic content disclosure when realistic AI visuals are used.
avoid: Claiming no AI was used.
Copying another channel's disclaimer text.
checks: The channel description carries the disclaimer before the first upload.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 session, p. 475 (owner course material, restated)

title: Music brief derived from the script
when: When background music is chosen for a video.
summary: Read the script and write a music brief: category, genre, mood, instrumental or vocal, the instruments that suit it, search keywords for licensed libraries, and the length needed. Licence terms are checked before anything is used.
steps: Category and genre that match the script.
Mood in one line, and where it should change.
Instrumental by default; name the instruments.
Search keywords for licensed libraries.
Duration per section.
avoid: Tracks without a recorded licence.
Vocals under narration.
checks: Each chosen track has its source, licence and attribution need recorded.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 4-5 (owner course material, restated)

title: When views stall: change prompts, thumbnails, then format
when: When impressions or views on a channel drop or stop growing.
summary: Early ups and downs are normal in the first month. If a stall persists, change the inputs in order: the prompts behind scripts and titles, then thumbnails, then the editing format. Never delete and re-upload the same content.
steps: Check whether the channel is still in its first month; if so, keep publishing and watch.
If the stall persists, revise script and title prompts first.
Then test new thumbnails.
Then switch to another approved editing format.
avoid: Deleting videos and re-uploading the same content to a new channel; that invites reused-content and circumvention enforcement.
Workarounds with extra devices, networks or accounts to evade enforcement.
checks: The analytics note states which lever was changed and when.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 112, 437-438, 474 (owner course material, restated; evasion tactics excluded)

title: Guardrails against inauthentic and reused content
when: Whenever a family plans a series, and at every review before upload.
summary: Faceless channels are judged on whether each video adds real value. Topics come from credible sources, titles vary, scripts carry original research and the owner's view, visuals are not one image repeated, formats rotate, and the title and thumbnail are decided before production. Since July 2025 YouTube calls this the inauthentic-content policy: mass-produced or templated videos risk losing monetisation, which matters most for a program that makes many videos.
do: Choose topics that serve real interests and rest on credible sources.
Vary title structures across the channel.
Write scripts from original research with added insight.
Settle title and thumbnail before production starts.
Rotate editing formats within the niche.
Make every video in a series differ in substance: its own research, structure and visual design, not only a new topic word.
avoid: Single-image videos as a channel's standard format.
One title structure across a channel's whole catalogue.
Celebrity avatars or likeness as the channel's draw.
Content with no human insight, data or perspective.
Device, network, account or payment-identity tactics meant to get around YouTube enforcement.
checks: titleVariationIssues is clean for the channel's recent titles.
The script cites its sources and carries the owner's angle.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 notes, pp. 437-441, 473-475 (owner course material, restated; circumvention tactics excluded); updated 0.71 from claude-youtube (MIT, 84c3fa6): references/monetization-guide.md

title: Profile: calm history for sleep
when: Pin to a family making long, calm history narration that helps viewers relax or sleep.
summary: Viewers want to learn and drift off at once. Lengths run from one to several hours, the voice is a gentle historian, and the contrast is the comfort of narration against the hardship of the past.

numbers.audience: 18-45, history lovers, slightly female-skewed for daily-life history
numbers.contrast: comfort of narration vs hardship of the era
numbers.title_style: plain promise of calm plus the full story; sleep words varied, no competitor signature phrase
numbers.visual_look: classical oil painting or softly tinted archival imagery

do: Use sleep-intent words naturally: drift off, relax, quiet night, bedtime.
avoid: Copying another channel's fixed title formula word for word.
checks: Titles avoid any one competitor's signature wording.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 35-40, 113-120, 167-200, 303-315 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: mystery, lost knowledge and ancient puzzles for sleep
when: Pin to a family making long, calm narration about unsolved history and ancient puzzles.
summary: Late-night viewers want controlled curiosity: intrigue without anxiety. Mystery must stay honest, so speculation is labelled as speculation and real evidence is named.

numbers.audience: 18-44, curious late-night listeners; one course profile reads majority female 25-45 professionals
numbers.contrast: what we thought vs what we now know; evidence vs speculation
numbers.visual_look: cinematic ancient sites, golden and deep blue light, soft fog, no text

avoid: Presenting conspiracy or 'forbidden truth' framing as fact.
Inventing expert reactions.
checks: Each mystery states what is known, what is claimed and who claims it.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 121-130, 173-200, 303-315 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: cosmic science and philosophy of physics
when: Pin to a family making long documentaries on space, physics and consciousness for awe-driven viewers.
summary: The audience wants wonder that holds up. Move from a hook through scientific foundations, debates and speculative horizons to philosophical closure, and keep the line between established science and speculation visible.

numbers.audience: 18-45, science and philosophy enthusiasts, many listening at bedtime
numbers.structure: hook, foundations, debates, speculative horizons, philosophical closure
numbers.contrast: science vs speculation, evidence vs mystery
numbers.visual_look: deep-space photography style, observatories, scientific visualisation

avoid: Stating speculative physics as settled.
Misquoting scientists.
checks: Speculative passages are signposted as speculation.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 145-148, 189-193, 233-252, 270-277, 336-345 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: dark philosophy, psychology and self-mastery
when: Pin to a family making authoritative philosophy and psychology essays on power, discipline and human nature.
summary: Viewers want to feel more perceptive and in control. Ground every idea in a named thinker or study, keep the tone composed rather than aggressive, and deliver a usable insight.

numbers.audience: mostly men 18-40, plus misunderstood or burnt-out viewers 18-45
numbers.contrast: weakness vs mastery, appearance vs reality
numbers.visual_look: expressive oil sketch or symbolic classical imagery

avoid: Generalisations that demean women, men or any group.
Manipulation advice aimed at harming others.
checks: Each idea names its source thinker or study.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 23-28, 201-205, 220-226, 278-282 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: Stoic philosophy for everyday life
when: Pin to a family making Stoic philosophy videos for self-improvement viewers.
summary: Viewers want calm control and practical wisdom. Quote the Stoics accurately, translate each idea into a present-day situation, and finish with an empowering or relaxing close.

numbers.audience: adults 25-45 seeking emotional control and personal growth
numbers.title_styles: practical and direct, or transformative and intriguing

avoid: Quotes attributed to a Stoic without a source.
checks: Every quotation is attributed to a work.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 253-261, 316-327 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: spiritual psychology and inner healing
when: Pin to a family making reflective spiritual and Jungian psychology videos for people healing from hard relationships.
summary: Viewers want to feel seen and steadier. Validate without flattering, explain psychological ideas accurately, and offer reflection rather than promises.

numbers.audience: 25-55, often women, healing from difficult families or relationships, late-night introspective viewers
numbers.arc: hook, validation, understanding, transformation, empowerment, community
numbers.visual_look: divine, cinematic, symbolic imagery with soft light

avoid: Telling viewers they are chosen or superior to others.
Health, financial or manifestation outcomes presented as guaranteed.
Psychological terms used loosely or misattributed to Jung.
checks: No sentence promises a guaranteed outcome.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 99-104, 214-219, 262-269, 375-380 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: archaeological discoveries
when: Pin to a family making long documentaries about real archaeological finds.
summary: Curious, educated viewers want new findings explained well. Lead with one real discovery, support it with related finds, then context and the open questions, and name the researchers and institutions involved.
avoid: Inventing a discovery, a quote or a researcher's reaction.
Claims that technology 'should not exist' without evidence.
checks: Each discovery cites a publication, institution or report.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 105-111 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: military history (ancient and modern)
when: Pin to a family making military history documentaries, from Rome to the Second World War.
summary: Strategy-minded viewers want decisions explained, not only battles described. Mix tactical analysis with the people involved, use accurate terms, and treat the human cost with seriousness.

numbers.audience: 25-55, history and strategy fans, mostly men
numbers.visual_look: period-accurate legions or true black-and-white 1940s archival look

avoid: Glorifying violence or any regime.
Identifiable real people generated by AI.
checks: Dates, units and places match a cited source.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 13-22, 139-144, 381-392 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: true crime from public records
when: Pin to a family making documentaries about real, closed criminal cases.
summary: Viewers want suspense and truth together. Every case is real and verifiable through court judgments, prosecution or agency releases and established news; titles use the case's own specifics, never the background of the people involved.

numbers.audience: 18-45 viewers of crime documentaries and justice stories
numbers.sources: court judgments, prosecution and national crime agency releases, national archives, established news

avoid: Titles or framing built on ethnicity, nationality or immigration status.
Unverified cases or composite stories presented as real.
checks: Each case lists at least one primary and one news source.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 132-136 (owner course material, restated; ethnicity title formula excluded)

title: Profile: horror narration and dark folklore
when: Pin to a family making calm, atmospheric horror stories and folklore narration.
summary: Listeners want calm dread: tension that builds through sensory detail rather than jump scares. Fiction is labelled as fiction, and folklore is told as folklore.

numbers.visual_look: low-light cinematic suspense, or wet-plate black-and-white for period folklore

avoid: Taboo or degrading title hooks that put monetisation at risk.
Realistic fake evidence such as invented case files presented as real.
checks: Fictional stories are labelled as fiction in the description.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 394-403, 413-429 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: nostalgia for older viewers
when: Pin to a family making reflective videos about everyday life from the 1950s to the 1990s.
summary: Older viewers want warm recognition and the pride of having lived it. Blend memory with real history, keep the pace calm, and let small details do the work.

numbers.audience: 40-75, Boomers, Generation X and older Millennials
numbers.visual_look: vintage hand-painted illustration with muted colours

avoid: Mocking the present to flatter the past.
checks: Each remembered detail is accurate to its decade.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 404-412 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: betrayal-and-revenge drama stories
when: Pin to a family making fictional relationship drama narrated as long stories.
summary: Viewers want an emotional arc they can settle into: betrayal, suffering, revelation, reversal, triumph and closure. It is fiction and must be presented as fiction.

numbers.audience: women 18-45 who enjoy soap-opera and bedtime drama
numbers.arc: betrayal, suffering, revelation, reversal, triumph, closure
numbers.contrast: cruelty vs calm dignity, despair vs empowerment

avoid: Presenting invented stories as real events.
Abuse described for shock.
checks: The description labels the story as fiction.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 366-374 (owner course material, restated)

title: Profile: cozy original fantasy for sleep
when: Pin to a family making calm, cozy fantasy-world narration for bedtime.
summary: Fans of beloved fantasy worlds want the feeling of those places: warmth, nostalgia, safety. Build an original world that evokes the mood, and never retell, quote or name a protected franchise.

numbers.angles: atmosphere, experience, emotion and format, one per core idea

avoid: Franchise names, characters, places or dialogue.
Retelling scenes from published books or films.
checks: No title, script or prompt contains a franchise's protected names.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, 2026 session, pp. 445-446 (owner course material, restated with franchise use excluded)

title: Profile: fast-cut self-improvement
when: Pin to a family making short, energetic self-improvement videos with rapid visual changes.
summary: Viewers want quick, usable change. Scripts are around 1,000 words from problem to action, and the edit changes picture every few seconds with clear on-screen emphasis.

numbers.audience: young adults working on focus, discipline and habits

avoid: Stacking fear-of-missing-out lines in every section.
Unsupported claims about the brain or health.
checks: Every technique is concrete enough to try the same day.
source: CB YT AI Mastery Prompts Bundle, pp. 51-62 (owner course material, restated)
